FleetOpt: Analytical Fleet Provisioning for LLM Inference
with Compress-and-Route as Implementation Mechanism

Huamin Chen Affiliation: vLLM Semantic Router Project    Xunzhuo Liu Affiliation: vLLM Semantic Router Project    Yuhan Liu Affiliation: University of Chicago    Junchen Jiang Affiliation: Tensormesh Inc / UChicago    Bowei He ††thanks: Corresponding author: Bowei.He@mbzuai.ac.ae Affiliation: MBZUAI / McGill University    Xue Liu Affiliation: MBZUAI / McGill University
2026
Abstract

Modern LLM GPU fleets are provisioned for worst-case context lengths that the vast majority of requests never approach, wasting GPU capacity on idle KV-cache slots. We present FleetOpt, a framework that starts from first principles: given a workload’s prompt-length CDF and a P99 TTFT target, derive the minimum-cost fleet analytically, then deploy it in practice.

The analytical core models each pool as an M/G/cc queue and derives that the minimum-cost fleet is a two-pool architecture — a short-context pool 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s} and a long-context pool 𝒫l\mathcal{P}_{l} — with an optimal boundary Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} satisfying an equal marginal GPU cost condition across both pools. The fundamental barrier to achieving Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} is the cost cliff: a hard routing step where requests just above Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} consume 8×8\times–42×42\times more GPU capacity than requests just below it (depending on the context window ratio), creating a structural disincentive to lower the boundary.

Compress-and-Route (C&R) is the implementation mechanism that resolves this barrier. Gateway-layer extractive compression trims borderline requests below Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} before the engine ever sees them, converting the hard hardware boundary into a software parameter read from the workload CDF. The two components are unified in the FleetOpt offline planner: given a CDF and SLO, it returns the optimal (ns∗,nl∗,Bshort∗,γ∗)(n_{s}^{*},n_{l}^{*},B_{\text{short}}^{*},\gamma^{*}) in under 1 ms.

On three production traces, the combined framework reduces total GPU cost by 6–82% versus a homogeneous fleet, with C&R contributing 1–44 percentage points beyond plain pool routing depending on workload archetype. The analytical model is validated against a discrete-event simulator (inference-fleet-sim) with ≤3%\leq 3\% error on predicted GPU utilization across all pools and workloads.

1 Introduction

Modern LLMs support context windows of 128K tokens or more, yet production traces reveal a persistent mismatch: in the Azure LLM Inference Trace, 80% of requests use fewer than 2K tokens (Patel et al., 2024; Zhang and Shen, 2024; Agrawal et al., 2024c). A homogeneous fleet provisioned for worst-case context length allocates KV-cache capacity that goes almost entirely unused for the vast majority of requests. Pool routing (Chen et al., 2026b) addresses this by splitting the fleet into short- and long-context pools, cutting GPU cost by 16–38% in scenarios studied by prior work.

The residual problem: the cost cliff.

Even with pool routing, a structural inefficiency remains at the pool boundary BshortB_{\text{short}}. The routing decision is binary: a request at Ltotal=BshortL_{\text{total}}=B_{\text{short}} fills one of nmax(s)n_{\max}^{(s)} short-pool slots; a request one token longer must enter the long pool, which offers only nmax(l)=16n_{\max}^{(l)}=16 slots per GPU — a throughput-capacity penalty of 8×8\times–42×42\times for a single token (Section 2.2). Requests in the borderline band (Bshort,γ​Bshort](B_{\text{short}},\,\gamma B_{\text{short}}] are not genuinely long; they are RAG payloads with one extra paragraph, or multi-turn sessions whose history just crossed the threshold. For the workloads we study, 4.6–11.2% of all traffic falls in this band. Each borderline request is assigned a long-pool slot provisioned for 64K tokens while using at most 1/ρ1/\rho of its KV budget.

Our approach: analytical model first, then implement.

Prior work treats pool routing and Compress-and-Route (C&R) as independent operational interventions: deploy pool routing, then optionally retrofit C&R on the existing fleet. This framing leaves value on the table.

We take a different path. We start from the analytical optimum: given a workload CDF and a P99 TTFT target, what is the minimum-cost fleet? The M/G/cc queuing model answers this precisely: a two-pool architecture with a specific boundary Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*}. But the cost cliff is a barrier to achieving Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} — lowering the boundary forces borderline requests to the expensive long pool.

C&R is the implementation mechanism that resolves this barrier. By compressing borderline requests below Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} at the gateway, C&R makes the analytically-optimal boundary achievable in practice. The combined framework does not merely retrofit compression onto an existing fleet; it provisions the correct fleet from the start, using C&R to enforce the boundary the model prescribes.

Key results.

  1. 1.

    The minimum-cost fleet is analytically derived. Under the M/G/cc model (with server count c=ngpus×nmaxc=n_{\text{gpus}}\times n_{\max} KV slots), the optimal two-pool fleet satisfies an equal marginal GPU cost condition across both pools. GPU counts come from Erlang-C inversion at each pool’s arrival rate and service distribution (Section 3).

  2. 2.

    The cost cliff is a barrier to achieving Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} without compression. At the optimal boundary, the borderline band contains 43–76% of above-threshold traffic for real workloads (4.6–11.2% of all traffic). Without compression, the operator must either raise BshortB_{\text{short}} (losing savings) or over-provision the long pool (paying more) to absorb borderline load.

  3. 3.

    C&R converts the hard boundary into a software knob. Gateway-layer extractive compression trims borderline prompts in 2–7 ms. The compressed token budget is chosen so KV overflow is impossible by construction (Section 5). The effective routing boundary shifts from BshortB_{\text{short}} to γ​Bshort\gamma B_{\text{short}}, where γ∗\gamma^{*} comes from the planner sweep.

  4. 4.

    Combined savings: 6–82% vs. homogeneous. On three production traces, the FleetOpt framework achieves 6.7–82.4% GPU cost reduction versus homogeneous deployment. C&R contributes an incremental 1.2 pp (Agent-heavy), 15.9 pp (LMSYS), and 43.7 pp (Azure) beyond plain pool routing (Section 7).

  5. 5.

    Analytical model validated by DES. inference-fleet-sim (Chen et al., 2026c) confirms analytical GPU utilization predictions match simulation within 3% across all workloads and pools, operating in the many-server regime where queueing delays are negligible.

Paper organization.

Section 2 characterizes the cost cliff and workload archetypes. Section 3 develops the analytical fleet model. Section 4 derives optimal fleet sizing and the optimal boundary. Section 5 presents C&R as the implementation mechanism. Section 6 gives the FleetOpt offline planner. Section 7 evaluates on production traces. Sections 8 and 9 discuss related work and conclude.

2 Background: The Cost Cliff and Workload Archetypes

2.1 Pool Routing Basics

A request rr is assigned a total token budget Ltotal=⌈|r|/c^k⌉+r.max_output_tokensL_{\text{total}}=\lceil|r|/\hat{c}_{k}\rceil+r.\texttt{max\_output\_tokens}, where c^k\hat{c}_{k} is a per-category bytes-per-token EMA estimate. Pool routing routes rr to 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s} if Ltotal≤BshortL_{\text{total}}\leq B_{\text{short}}, else 𝒫l\mathcal{P}_{l}. The short pool is sized for Cmax(s)C_{\max}^{(s)} tokens (e.g., 8K) with nmax(s)n_{\max}^{(s)} concurrent sequences per GPU; the long pool for Cmax(l)C_{\max}^{(l)} tokens (e.g., 64K) with nmax(l)n_{\max}^{(l)}.

2.2 KV-Cache Memory and the Cost Cliff

For Llama-3-70B in fp16, the KV cache grows at 320 KB per token across 80 layers. A long-pool slot sized for 64K tokens requires 64,000×320​KB≈20.564{,}000\times 320\,\text{KB}\approx 20.5 GB of GPU memory; the same hardware configured for 8K can host ρ=8×\rho=8\times as many concurrent sequences, delivering ρ=8×\rho=8\times the throughput. The GPU savings formula for pool routing is α⁡(1−1/ρ)\alpha(1-1/\rho) (Chen et al., 2026b), where α\alpha is the fraction of traffic routed to 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s}.

The cost cliff is the discontinuity at BshortB_{\text{short}}: a request at Bshort+1B_{\text{short}}+1 tokens must enter the long pool, which hosts only nmax(l)=16n_{\max}^{(l)}=16 concurrent slots per GPU (sized for 64K tokens), versus nmax(s)n_{\max}^{(s)} short-pool slots. The cliff ratio ρ=nmax(s)/nmax(l)\rho=n_{\max}^{(s)}/n_{\max}^{(l)} depends on the short-pool context window: ρ=8×\rho=8\times at Bshort=8,192B_{\text{short}}=8{,}192, ρ=16×\rho=16\times at Bshort=4,096B_{\text{short}}=4{,}096, and ρ=42×\rho=42\times at Bshort=1,536B_{\text{short}}=1{,}536 (Table 2). A borderline request at 1.1×Bshort1.1\times B_{\text{short}} uses only 1/ρ1/\rho of the long-pool KV budget it was allocated. This is not a flaw of pool routing; it is the unavoidable consequence of provisioning slots for worst-case context length. The only escape is to keep requests below BshortB_{\text{short}}.

2.3 The Borderline Band

The borderline band (Bshort,γ​Bshort](B_{\text{short}},\,\gamma B_{\text{short}}] contains requests whose prompts exceed BshortB_{\text{short}} only slightly and could be compressed below BshortB_{\text{short}} at bandwidth ratio γ\gamma. Let α=F⁡(Bshort)\alpha=F(B_{\text{short}}) (the fraction of requests already in 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s}) and β=F⁡(γ​Bshort)−F⁡(Bshort)\beta=F(\gamma B_{\text{short}})-F(B_{\text{short}}) (the borderline fraction). Table 2 shows β\beta across workloads.

2.4 Workload CDF Archetypes

Three qualitatively different workload shapes determine how the cost cliff manifests and which remediation is appropriate.

Archetype I (Concentrated-below). The CDF has a sharp knee below BshortB_{\text{short}}: F⁡(Bshort)≥0.90F(B_{\text{short}})\geq 0.90 and the density f⁡(Bshort)f(B_{\text{short}}) is high. The borderline fraction β\beta is moderate in absolute terms (4.6–7.8%), but the fraction-of-above-threshold traffic that is borderline is large (51–76%). Pool routing already captures most savings; C&R provides meaningful additional savings because the cliff ratio ρ\rho is large (16×16\times–42×42\times).

Archetype II (Dispersed). The CDF spreads across two or more decades of token counts. Significant borderline traffic exists (β=7\beta=7–12%12\%), and C&R provides meaningful incremental savings. The agent-heavy trace (RAG + tool-use + code) is the primary representative.

Archetype III (Concentrated-above). The mass of the distribution lies above BshortB_{\text{short}} (e.g., code-agent tasks at 10–50K tokens). The borderline fraction is negligible; the dominant lever is raising BshortB_{\text{short}} before any compression.

3 Analytical Fleet Model

3.1 Queueing Model

We model each pool as an M/G/cc queue. Let λ\lambda be the total fleet arrival rate. After routing:

λs\displaystyle\lambda_{s} =α′​λ,where ​α′=α+β​pc\displaystyle=\alpha^{\prime}\,\lambda,\quad\text{where }\alpha^{\prime}=\alpha+\beta p_{c} (1)
λl\displaystyle\lambda_{l} =(1−α′)​λ\displaystyle=(1-\alpha^{\prime})\,\lambda (2)

Here α=F⁡(Bshort)\alpha=F(B_{\text{short}}), β=F⁡(γ​Bshort)−F⁡(Bshort)\beta=F(\gamma B_{\text{short}})-F(B_{\text{short}}) is the borderline fraction, and pc∈[0,1]p_{c}\in[0,1] is the compressibility rate (fraction of borderline requests successfully compressed).

Service time model.

GPU iteration latency under continuous batching is

titer=W+H⋅nslots,t_{\text{iter}}=W+H\cdot n_{\text{slots}}, (3)

where W=8W=8 ms (baseline compute for Llama-3-70B/A100) and H=0.65H=0.65 ms/slot (per-slot memory-bandwidth cost) are hardware constants calibrated to the A100-80GB. Under continuous batching, all nmaxn_{\max} slots advance in lockstep each iteration. A request with LinL_{\text{in}} input tokens and LoutL_{\text{out}} output tokens occupies a slot for

𝔼⁡[S]=(⌈Lin/Cchunk⌉+Lout)⋅titer,\mathbb{E}[S]=\bigl(\lceil L_{\text{in}}/C_{\text{chunk}}\rceil+L_{\text{out}}\bigr)\cdot t_{\text{iter}}, (4)

wall-clock seconds (chunk size Cchunk=512C_{\text{chunk}}=512). The GPU-level throughput is μgpu=nmax/𝔼⁡[S]\mu_{\text{gpu}}=n_{\max}/\mathbb{E}[S] requests per second; the squared coefficient of variation is Cs2=Var⁡[S]/(𝔼⁡[S])2C_{s}^{2}=\mathrm{Var}[S]/(\mathbb{E}[S])^{2}, estimated by Monte Carlo sampling from the pool’s request distribution.

M/G/cc tail-wait approximation.

We model a pool with nn GPUs as an M/G/cc queue with c=n⋅nmaxc=n\cdot n_{\max} total KV slots as servers, each with per-slot service rate μ=1/𝔼⁡[S]\mu=1/\mathbb{E}[S]. The offered load is ϱ=λp/(c​μ)<1\varrho=\lambda_{p}/(c\,\mu)<1. The Erlang-C probability (probability a new request must wait for a slot) is

C⁡(c,ϱ)=(c​ϱ)c/(c!​(1−ϱ))∑k=0c−1(c​ϱ)k/k!+(c​ϱ)c/(c!​(1−ϱ)),C(c,\varrho)=\frac{(c\varrho)^{c}/(c!\,(1-\varrho))}{\sum_{k=0}^{c-1}(c\varrho)^{k}/k!+(c\varrho)^{c}/(c!\,(1-\varrho))}, (5)

The Kimura (Kimura, 1994) M/G/cc approximation gives the P99 queue waiting time:

W99​(c,μ,Cs2)=ln⁡(C⁡(c,ϱ)/0.01)⋅(1+Cs2)2​(c​μ−λp).W_{99}(c,\mu,C_{s}^{2})=\frac{\ln\!\bigl(C(c,\varrho)/0.01\bigr)\cdot(1+C_{s}^{2})}{2\,(c\,\mu-\lambda_{p})}. (6)

In the many-server regime (c≫1c\gg 1), C⁡(c,ϱ)≈0C(c,\varrho)\approx 0 and W99≈0W_{99}\approx 0: slots are almost always available and queueing delays are negligible. Fleet sizing is then dominated by the utilization cap ρmax\rho_{\max} (Section 4.1).

3.2 TTFT Decomposition

Time-to-First-Token decomposes as

TTFT=Wqueue+Tprefill+Tfirst-decode,\text{TTFT}=W_{\text{queue}}+T_{\text{prefill}}+T_{\text{first-decode}}, (7)

where WqueueW_{\text{queue}} is the queueing delay before a slot is available, Tprefill=⌈Lin/Cchunk⌉⋅titerT_{\text{prefill}}=\lceil L_{\text{in}}/C_{\text{chunk}}\rceil\cdot t_{\text{iter}} is the physical prefill time (wall-clock, independent of batch size since all nmaxn_{\max} slots run in parallel), and Tfirst-decode=titerT_{\text{first-decode}}=t_{\text{iter}} is one decode step. The SLO constraint is

W99​(c,μ,Cs2)≤Tslo−Tprefill(99)−titer,W_{99}(c,\mu,C_{s}^{2})\;\leq\;T_{\text{slo}}-T_{\text{prefill}}^{(99)}-t_{\text{iter}}, (8)

where Tprefill(99)T_{\text{prefill}}^{(99)} is the P99 prefill time computed from the pool’s request length distribution.

3.3 Cost Model

GPU cost per unit time is csc_{s} per short-pool GPU and clc_{l} per long-pool GPU. Let ϕ=cl/cs\phi=c_{l}/c_{s} be the GPU cost ratio. Total annualized cost for a fleet of nsn_{s} and nln_{l} GPUs is

𝒞⁡(ns,nl)=cs​ns+cl​nl.\mathcal{C}(n_{s},n_{l})=c_{s}\,n_{s}+c_{l}\,n_{l}. (9)

The provisioning problem is

minns,nl∈ℤ>0⁡𝒞⁡(ns,nl)s.t. Eq. (8) holds for both pools.\min_{n_{s},\,n_{l}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}\mathcal{C}(n_{s},n_{l})\quad\text{s.t. Eq.~\eqref{eq:slo-constraint} holds for both pools.} (10)

4 Optimal Fleet Sizing

4.1 Per-Pool Sizing

Because the two pools are independent M/G/cc queues with fixed arrival rates λs\lambda_{s} and λl\lambda_{l}, problem (10) separates into two independent minimizations. For each pool, the minimum GPU count is

n∗=min⁡{c∈ℤ>0:W99​(c,μ,Cs2)≤Tslo,eff},n^{*}=\min\bigl\{c\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}:W_{99}(c,\mu,C_{s}^{2})\leq T_{\text{slo,eff}}\bigr\}, (11)

where Tslo,effT_{\text{slo,eff}} is the SLO budget after subtracting P99 prefill time per Eq. (8), and we additionally enforce n∗≥⌈λp/(ρmax​μ)⌉n^{*}\geq\lceil\lambda_{p}/(\rho_{\max}\mu)\rceil for a utilization cap ρmax=0.85\rho_{\max}=0.85 to ensure analytical stability.

4.2 The Cost Cliff Prevents Achieving Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*}

Differentiating total cost 𝒞\mathcal{C} with respect to BshortB_{\text{short}} and setting to zero (treating n∗n^{*} as a smooth function of λp\lambda_{p}) gives the first-order condition for the optimal boundary:

cs​∂ns∗∂λs=cl​∂nl∗∂λl.c_{s}\frac{\partial n_{s}^{*}}{\partial\lambda_{s}}=c_{l}\frac{\partial n_{l}^{*}}{\partial\lambda_{l}}. (12)

The λ​f​(Bshort)\lambda f(B_{\text{short}}) factor cancels from both sides, leaving the condition: the marginal cost of routing one additional request to the short pool must equal the marginal saving of removing one request from the long pool.

Proposition 1 (Optimal boundary — equal marginal GPU cost).

Under the M/G/cc cost model with ρmax\rho_{\max}-constrained sizing, the provisioning-optimal Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} satisfies Eq. (12): equal marginal GPU cost per unit traffic in both pools. For a homogeneous fleet (cs=clc_{s}=c_{l}, same GPU type), this holds when both pools operate at the same utilization level.

The problem: at any BshortB_{\text{short}}, the borderline band (Bshort,γ​Bshort](B_{\text{short}},\gamma B_{\text{short}}] contains 43–76% of above-threshold traffic for real workloads. Without a mechanism to redirect borderline requests to 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s}, the long pool must absorb this traffic at ρ=8\rho=8–42×42\times higher GPU cost per request, requiring significantly more GPUs than the analytical optimum. C&R resolves this by making the analytically-optimal boundary achievable in practice.

4.3 Optimal Compression Bandwidth γ∗\gamma^{*}

With C&R active, borderline requests at bandwidth γ\gamma are redirected to 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s}. The resulting α′=α+β​pc\alpha^{\prime}=\alpha+\beta p_{c} shifts λs\lambda_{s} upward and λl\lambda_{l} downward. The first-order condition for the optimal γ\gamma is:

cs​∂ns∗∂λs⋅pc⋅λ​f​(γ​Bshort)=cl​∂nl∗∂λl⋅pc⋅λ​f​(γ​Bshort),c_{s}\frac{\partial n_{s}^{*}}{\partial\lambda_{s}}\cdot p_{c}\cdot\lambda f(\gamma B_{\text{short}})=c_{l}\frac{\partial n_{l}^{*}}{\partial\lambda_{l}}\cdot p_{c}\cdot\lambda f(\gamma B_{\text{short}}), (13)

which again reduces to the equal marginal cost condition Eq. (12). In practice γ∗\gamma^{*} is found by discrete sweep over γ∈{1.0,1.1,…,2.0}\gamma\in\{1.0,1.1,\ldots,2.0\} because n∗n^{*} is integer-valued and the long-pool service rate must be recalibrated for the post-compression distribution at each γ\gamma. The sweep is fast (<1<1 ms). For workloads where most above-threshold traffic is borderline (Archetype I/II), γ∗\gamma^{*} tends toward large values (2.0), as compressing more traffic into 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s} reduces the expensive long pool. For Archetype II with a dispersed above-threshold distribution, γ∗\gamma^{*} reflects the balance between short-pool overheads and long-pool savings.

Theorem 2 (Co-design is never worse than retrofit).

Let 𝒞retro\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{retro}} be the cost of a fleet sized for pool routing at γ=1\gamma=1 with C&R later deployed, and 𝒞co\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{co}} be the cost of a fleet co-designed with C&R at the same γ\gamma. Then 𝒞co≤𝒞retro\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{co}}\leq\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{retro}}.

Proof sketch. The co-designed fleet solves the same minimization problem as the retrofitted fleet but with the additional freedom to reduce nl∗n_{l}^{*} knowing that λl\lambda_{l} will be lower. Hence the feasible set is larger and the minimum cost is weakly lower. □\square

5 Compress-and-Route as Implementation Mechanism

C&R is the gateway-layer component that makes Proposition 1’s optimal boundary achievable in practice. Rather than a separate system, it is the implementation of the optimal fleet boundary derived in Section 4.

5.1 The Virtual Pool

C&R shifts the effective routing boundary from BshortB_{\text{short}} to γ​Bshort\gamma B_{\text{short}} by compressing borderline requests at the gateway. A request rr with Bshort<Ltotal≤γ​BshortB_{\text{short}}<L_{\text{total}}\leq\gamma B_{\text{short}} is intercepted; its prompt is compressed to a token budget Tc=Bshort−LoutT_{c}=B_{\text{short}}-L_{\text{out}} and re-routed to 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s}. From the engine’s perspective, 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s} appears to have a higher effective CmaxC_{\max}: the virtual pool capacity is γ​Bshort\gamma B_{\text{short}} without any hardware change. The GPU savings gain is

Δ​α=β​pc,α′=α+β​pc,\Delta\alpha=\beta\,p_{c},\qquad\alpha^{\prime}=\alpha+\beta\,p_{c}, (14)

and additional GPU savings beyond pool routing are Δ​α​(1−1/ρ)=β​pc​(1−1/ρ)\Delta\alpha(1-1/\rho)=\beta p_{c}(1-1/\rho).

5.2 Extractive Compression Pipeline

The compressor is a pure classical-NLP extractive pipeline requiring no LLM inference. Given a borderline prompt xx and token budget Tc=Bshort−LoutT_{c}=B_{\text{short}}-L_{\text{out}}, it:

  1. 1.

    Splits xx into sentences with Unicode-aware heuristics.

  2. 2.

    Scores each sentence by a composite of TextRank (w=0.20w=0.20) (Mihalcea and Tarau, 2004), Position (w=0.40w=0.40), TF-IDF (w=0.35w=0.35) (Li et al., 2023a), and Novelty (w=0.05w=0.05).

  3. 3.

    Greedily selects sentences in score order, always retaining the first 3 and last 2 (primacy/recency invariant).

  4. 4.

    Stops when the cumulative token count reaches TcT_{c}.

Hard OOM guarantee.

The budget Tc=Bshort−LoutT_{c}=B_{\text{short}}-L_{\text{out}} is set by construction, so no compressed request can overflow 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s}’s KV cache:

Tc+Lout=Bshort.T_{c}+L_{\text{out}}=B_{\text{short}}. (15)

Content-type safety gate.

Compression is applied only to content categories where structural extraction is semantically safe: RAG and prose. Code is excluded. The category signal reuses the per-request EMA estimate from the base router at zero additional overhead.

Compression latency.

Measured on Intel Xeon Platinum 8568Y+, end-to-end compression takes 2–7 ms per borderline request. Weighted across all traffic, the mean overhead is ≤0.58\leq 0.58 ms per request.

Fidelity.

A fidelity study on 300 LMSYS-Chat-1M prompts from the Agent-heavy borderline band (Bshort=8,192B_{\text{short}}=8{,}192, γ=1.5\gamma=1.5, band 8K–12K tokens) gives compressibility pc=1.00p_{c}=1.00 for prose/RAG content, BERTScore F1 = 0.884, ROUGE-L recall = 0.856, and TF-IDF cosine similarity = 0.981 at a mean 15.4% token reduction (Appendix C). Code is excluded from compression.

6 The FleetOpt Offline Planner

Algorithm 1 gives the complete FleetOpt planner. It takes as input the workload CDF FF, arrival rate λ\lambda, SLO TsloT_{\text{slo}}, GPU profile (W,H,nmax(s),nmax(l),Cmax(s),Cmax(l))(W,H,n_{\max}^{(s)},n_{\max}^{(l)},C_{\max}^{(s)},C_{\max}^{(l)}), and cost ratio ϕ\phi. It returns the optimal (ns∗,nl∗,Bshort∗,γ∗)(n_{s}^{*},n_{l}^{*},B_{\text{short}}^{*},\gamma^{*}).

Candidate set ℬ\mathcal{B}. In practice BshortB_{\text{short}} is hardware-constrained: it determines nmax(s)=nmaxcalib×Ccalib/Bshortn_{\max}^{(s)}=n_{\max}^{\mathrm{calib}}\times C_{\text{calib}}/B_{\text{short}}, which must be a positive integer. The search is therefore over the finite set of CDF breakpoints that yield valid nmax(s)n_{\max}^{(s)} values (typically 5–15 candidates per workload). The total sweep — all B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B} times all γ\gamma — completes in under 1 ms. Proposition 1 provides the FOC that characterises Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} analytically; the sweep finds the integer-optimal solution consistent with hardware granularity.

Critical: μl\mu_{l} recalibration.

Step 6 recalibrates the long-pool service rate from the post-compression request distribution (requests with Ltotal>γ​Bshort∗L_{\text{total}}>\gamma B_{\text{short}}^{*}), not the full above-threshold distribution. Compressing borderline requests out of the long pool hardens the remaining distribution: longer mean token length, lower μl\mu_{l}. Skipping this recalibration systematically overestimates the savings from larger γ\gamma. With correct recalibration, the planner finds γ∗=2.0\gamma^{*}=2.0 for Archetype I/II workloads (Azure, LMSYS) where the long pool shrinks substantially, and γ∗=1.5\gamma^{*}=1.5 for the dispersed Agent-heavy workload where gains plateau.

Erlang-C inversion.

The minimum server count cc satisfying Eq. (8) is found by binary search over the interval [⌈a/ρmax⌉, 10​⌈a⌉][\lceil a/\rho_{\max}\rceil,\;10\lceil a\rceil] where a=λp/μgpua=\lambda_{p}/\mu_{\text{gpu}}, with utilization cap ρmax=0.85\rho_{\max}=0.85.

7 Evaluation

7.1 Setup

Workload traces.

We evaluate on two public traces and one synthetic trace built from published workload statistics.

Azure LLM Inference Trace 2023 (Patel et al., 2024) contains 28,185 requests (8,819 coding, 19,366 conversational). Mean Ltotal=1,588L_{\text{total}}=1{,}588 tokens; p90 = 4,242; p99 = 7,445. We use Bshort=4,096B_{\text{short}}=4{,}096 where α=0.898\alpha=0.898 and β=0.078\beta=0.078, giving a 16×\times cliff and a meaningful two-pool split (Archetype I/II).

LMSYS-Chat-1M (multi-turn) (Zheng et al., 2024) uses accumulated context at each turn. We use Bshort=1,536B_{\text{short}}=1{,}536 where α=0.909\alpha=0.909 and β=0.046\beta=0.046, giving a 42×\times cliff (Archetype I/II).

Agent-heavy is a synthetic trace derived from published statistics for SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) (40%), BFCL (Yan et al., 2024) (25%), and RAG pipelines (Lewis et al., 2020) (35%). Mean Ltotal=6,511L_{\text{total}}=6{,}511 tokens; p50 = 4,096; p90 = 16,384; p99 = 32,768. At Bshort=8,192B_{\text{short}}=8{,}192, α=0.740\alpha=0.740, β=0.112\beta=0.112 (Archetype II, the primary scenario for C&R benefit). The SWE-bench component consists largely of code; code requests are excluded from compression (Section 5.2). The effective compression success rate for Agent-heavy borderline traffic is pc=0.75p_{c}=0.75, reflecting that approximately 25% of borderline requests are code-category and cannot be compressed.

Simulation parameters.

W=8W=8 ms, H=0.65H=0.65 ms/slot, Cchunk=512C_{\text{chunk}}=512, calibrated to Llama-3-70B on A100-80GB (8-GPU tensor-parallel node). The long pool is sized for Cmax(l)=65,536C_{\max}^{(l)}=65{,}536 tokens, giving nmax(l)=16n_{\max}^{(l)}=16 concurrent slots per GPU and KV memory ≈20.0\approx 20.0 GB per slot (320 KB/token). Short-pool nmax(s)n_{\max}^{(s)} depends on BshortB_{\text{short}}: 256 at 4K, 682 at 1.5K, 128 at 8K. GPU cost $2.21/GPU-hr. Fleet arrival rate λ=1,000\lambda=1{,}000 req/s; P99 TTFT target Tslo=500T_{\text{slo}}=500 ms unless stated otherwise. DES validation uses inference-fleet-sim (Chen et al., 2026c).

Baselines.

  1. 1.

    Homogeneous: single pool sized for 64K context.

  2. 2.

    Pool routing (PR): two pools at workload-specific BshortB_{\text{short}} (Table 2), γ=1.0\gamma=1.0 (no compression).

  3. 3.

    PR + C&R (retrofit): C&R at γ=1.5\gamma=1.5 deployed on the PR fleet, co-sized for the compressed λs\lambda_{s}.

  4. 4.

    FleetOpt (co-design): fleet co-designed by Algorithm 1 at optimal γ∗\gamma^{*}.

7.2 Fleet GPU Savings vs. Homogeneous

Table 3 shows fleet GPU counts and GPU savings versus the homogeneous baseline. The FleetOpt fleet is the outcome of the complete framework: optimal analytical sizing plus C&R.

Savings decomposition.

The numbers in Table 3 follow a clear pattern. Pool routing alone saves 5.5–41.7%, with the biggest gains when α\alpha is high and the cliff ratio ρ\rho is large. C&R with γ=1.5\gamma=1.5 adds 29 percentage points for Azure (because β=7.8%\beta=7.8\% moves 76% of above-threshold traffic into the efficient short pool, and ρ=16×\rho=16\times makes each redirected request highly valuable) but only 1.2 pp for Agent-heavy (because 26% of all traffic remains above γ​Bshort\gamma B_{\text{short}}, requiring a large long pool regardless). FleetOpt at γ∗=2.0\gamma^{*}=2.0 for Azure nearly eliminates the long pool (2 GPUs), achieving 82.4% savings.

When does C&R add value?

The incremental GPU saving from adding C&R to pool routing is Δ​α​(1−1/ρ)=β​pc​(1−nmax(l)/nmax(s))\Delta\alpha(1-1/\rho)=\beta p_{c}(1-n_{\max}^{(l)}/n_{\max}^{(s)}). This is large when the borderline fraction β\beta is significant and the cliff ratio ρ\rho is large. For Agent-heavy, β=11.2%\beta=11.2\% is moderate but ρ=8×\rho=8\times is the smallest cliff, and pc=0.75p_{c}=0.75 (code exclusion), limiting the per-request gain. For Azure, β=7.8%\beta=7.8\% paired with ρ=16×\rho=16\times yields large incremental gains.

Why co-design equals retrofit for Agent-heavy.

Table 3 shows that for Agent-heavy, the PR+C&R retrofit at γ=1.5\gamma=1.5 and FleetOpt at γ∗=1.5\gamma^{*}=1.5 produce identical fleets. This is expected: when the planner’s optimal γ∗\gamma^{*} matches the retrofit’s γ\gamma, the two approaches arrive at the same (ns,nl)(n_{s},n_{l}) by construction. Theorem 2 is satisfied (co-design ≤\leq retrofit), but the inequality is tight. The co-design advantage is largest when γ∗\gamma^{*} exceeds the retrofit’s γ\gamma, which occurs when most above-threshold traffic is borderline (Archetype I/II, Azure and LMSYS). For Agent-heavy (Archetype II with dispersed above-threshold traffic), γ∗=1.5\gamma^{*}=1.5 is already the practical limit: compressing further leaves a harder long-pool distribution and yields no net saving.

7.3 Compression Pipeline Latency

The compressor is applied only to borderline requests, so the mean overhead per request is β×tcompress\beta\times t_{\text{compress}}. Table 4 shows the latency profile.

Even in the worst case (agent-heavy), the 0.39 ms average overhead is invisible against a 500 ms TTFT budget.

7.4 Analytical Model Validation

We validate the FleetOpt analytical model against inference-fleet-sim (Chen et al., 2026c), an open-source discrete-event simulator for heterogeneous LLM GPU fleets. The simulator drives Poisson arrivals from the empirical CDF with λ=1,000\lambda=1{,}000 req/s and records the fraction of slot-time that KV-cache slots are busy (GPU utilization ρ^\hat{\rho}).

Table 5 compares the analytical utilization ρana=λp/(n⋅μgpu)\rho_{\text{ana}}=\lambda_{p}/(n\cdot\mu_{\text{gpu}}) against the DES-measured ρ^\hat{\rho} for the pool-routing (γ=1\gamma=1) fleet from Table 3.

The analytical model predicts GPU utilization within 3% of the DES across all pools and workloads. Both analytical and DES values sit near ρmax=0.85\rho_{\max}=0.85, confirming that the ρmax\rho_{\max}-constrained sizing hits its target. The analytical model is slightly optimistic: actual utilization runs 0.1–2.7% above prediction in all cases. In practice this means the provisioned fleet is just barely busier than expected; adding 1–3 GPUs per pool eliminates even this small gap.

These fleets operate in the many-server regime: total KV slots c=n⋅nmaxc=n\cdot n_{\max} ranges from 112 to 32,592 across our configurations. At that scale the Erlang-C probability C⁡(c,ϱ)≪1C(c,\varrho)\ll 1, slot-wait times are negligible, and fleet sizing is dominated entirely by the utilization cap ρmax\rho_{\max}. In this regime the full M/G/cc + Kimura apparatus reduces to the simpler bound n∗≈⌈λp/(ρmax​μ)⌉n^{*}\approx\lceil\lambda_{p}/(\rho_{\max}\mu)\rceil; the queueing machinery becomes load-bearing only for smaller, lightly-provisioned fleets (few GPUs, high ϱ\varrho).

P99 TTFT. Because queue waits are negligible, TTFT is dominated by prefill time. Analytical P99 TTFT for the PR fleet: Azure short 20 ms / long 80 ms; LMSYS short 11 ms / long 48 ms; Agent-heavy short 47 ms / long 220 ms — all comfortably within the 500 ms SLO. The FleetOpt planner enforces the SLO constraint (Eq. (8)) directly; in the many-server regime this constraint is non-binding and the 500 ms SLO is met with large margin across all configurations.

7.5 Arrival-Rate Sensitivity

Table 6 shows how fleet sizes scale with arrival rate for the Agent-heavy workload. The savings from pool routing (5.4–5.5%) and FleetOpt (6.2–6.8%) are stable across a 20×\times range of arrival rates, confirming that the proportional GPU savings from the two-pool architecture scale linearly with load.

8 Related Work

Pool routing and length-specialized serving.

Chen et al. (2026b) establishes pool routing and the GPU savings formula α⁡(1−1/ρ)\alpha(1-1/\rho). Yuan et al. (2025) independently validates length-specialized partitioning. She et al. (2026) and Agrawal et al. (2024a) address length heterogeneity at the engine layer; this paper addresses the upstream provisioning decision.

Prompt compression as routing lever.

Chen et al. (2026a) first uses prompt compression as an operational fleet routing lever, studying C&R as a retrofit on a fixed fleet. Here we treat C&R as the implementation mechanism for the analytically-derived optimal fleet boundary. The two are complementary: the analytical model prescribes Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*}, and C&R makes it achievable without hardware changes.

LLM capacity planning.

Romero et al. (2021) and Gujarati et al. (2020) study model-variant selection and predictive scaling, respectively. Patel et al. (2024) analyzes prefill/decode disaggregation but does not optimize fleet size jointly with routing. FleetOpt is the first system to jointly derive the optimal pool boundary and GPU counts from a workload CDF.

Queueing models for serving.

The M/G/cc queue and Erlang-C formula are classical (Harchol-Balter, 2013). Shahrad et al. (2020) applies queueing to serverless cold-start; Li et al. (2023b) to model placement. FleetOpt applies M/G/cc to the pool routing + compression joint provisioning problem, with the Kimura (Kimura, 1994) correction for service-time variance.

Fleet-level LLM simulation.

Vidur (Agrawal et al., 2024b) and similar tools simulate single inference engine instances. inference-fleet-sim (Chen et al., 2026c) provides fleet-level DES for heterogeneous multi-pool deployments and is used here to validate the FleetOpt analytical model.

9 Conclusion

Provisioning LLM GPU fleets for worst-case context lengths is expensive and largely avoidable. FleetOpt tackles this by starting from first principles: derive the minimum-cost fleet analytically, then build it.

The analytical core (M/G/cc queuing model with c=n⋅nmaxc=n\cdot n_{\max} total KV slots, Erlang-C inversion) shows that the optimal fleet is a two-pool architecture whose boundary Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} satisfies an equal marginal GPU cost condition. The fundamental barrier to achieving Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} in practice is the cost cliff: borderline requests at the optimal boundary pay ρ=8\rho=8–42×42\times the throughput cost of requests just below it. Compress-and-Route (C&R) resolves this barrier by compressing borderline prompts at the gateway, converting a hardware constraint into a software parameter.

The combined framework saves 6–82% in GPU cost versus homogeneous deployment, depending on the workload archetype and cliff ratio. Pool routing alone saves 5.5–41.7%; C&R adds 1.2–43.7 percentage points beyond pool routing. The largest gains arise when β\beta is significant and the cliff ratio ρ\rho is large: Azure at Bshort=4,096B_{\text{short}}=4{,}096 achieves 82.4% savings with ρ=16×\rho=16\times and γ∗=2.0\gamma^{*}=2.0. For Agent-heavy at Bshort=8,192B_{\text{short}}=8{,}192 with ρ=8×\rho=8\times, gains are more modest (6.7%) because 26% of traffic remains above γ​Bshort\gamma B_{\text{short}}.

How much C&R co-design adds beyond pool routing depends on three factors: the cliff ratio ρ\rho, the borderline fraction β\beta, and compressibility pcp_{c}. None of these can be read off a GPU spec sheet; they require a calibrated workload CDF and the recalibration of μl\mu_{l} for the post-compression distribution. inference-fleet-sim (Chen et al., 2026c) validates this within 3% utilization error. Skipping the recalibration leads to over-optimistic savings estimates and under-provisioned fleets.

The FleetOpt planner outputs the optimal (ns∗,nl∗,Bshort∗,γ∗)(n_{s}^{*},n_{l}^{*},B_{\text{short}}^{*},\gamma^{*}) in under 1 ms, making it practical to re-run whenever the workload CDF shifts.

Appendix A Erlang-C Inversion: Algorithm and Numerical Stability

The minimum feasible GPU count n∗n^{*} is found by binary search over cc using the numerically stable recursive Erlang-C form:

C⁡(c,ϱ)=11+(1−ϱ)⋅c!⋅∑k=0c−1(c​ϱ)k−ck!,C(c,\varrho)=\frac{1}{1+(1-\varrho)\cdot c!\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{c-1}\frac{(c\varrho)^{k-c}}{k!}}, (16)

computed in log-space to avoid overflow at large cc. The utilization cap ρmax=0.85\rho_{\max}=0.85 ensures we always search above the point where the Kimura approximation loses accuracy and the Erlang-C formula diverges near ϱ→1\varrho\to 1.

Appendix B Proof of Proposition 1

Total cost as a function of BshortB_{\text{short}}: 𝒞⁡(Bshort)=cs​ns∗​(F⁡(Bshort)​λ)+cl​nl∗​((1−F⁡(Bshort))​λ)\mathcal{C}(B_{\text{short}})=c_{s}n_{s}^{*}(F(B_{\text{short}})\lambda)+c_{l}n_{l}^{*}((1-F(B_{\text{short}}))\lambda). Differentiating with respect to BshortB_{\text{short}} and applying the chain rule:

d​𝒞d​Bshort=λ​f​(Bshort)​[cs​∂ns∗∂λs−cl​∂nl∗∂λl].\frac{d\mathcal{C}}{dB_{\text{short}}}=\lambda f(B_{\text{short}})\left[c_{s}\frac{\partial n_{s}^{*}}{\partial\lambda_{s}}-c_{l}\frac{\partial n_{l}^{*}}{\partial\lambda_{l}}\right]. (17)

Since λ​f​(Bshort)>0\lambda f(B_{\text{short}})>0 for any interior boundary, the FOC d​𝒞/d​Bshort=0d\mathcal{C}/dB_{\text{short}}=0 requires the bracketed term to be zero:

cs​∂ns∗∂λs=cl​∂nl∗∂λl.c_{s}\frac{\partial n_{s}^{*}}{\partial\lambda_{s}}=c_{l}\frac{\partial n_{l}^{*}}{\partial\lambda_{l}}. (18)

This is an equal marginal GPU cost condition: the marginal GPU cost of routing one additional request-per-second to the short pool equals the marginal GPU saving from removing one request-per-second from the long pool.

For a homogeneous fleet (cs=clc_{s}=c_{l}, same GPU type), the condition simplifies to ∂ns∗/∂λs=∂nl∗/∂λl\partial n_{s}^{*}/\partial\lambda_{s}=\partial n_{l}^{*}/\partial\lambda_{l}. Under the ρmax\rho_{\max}-constrained sizing regime (which dominates in practice as shown in Section 7.4): n∗≈⌈λp/(ρmax​μ)⌉n^{*}\approx\lceil\lambda_{p}/(\rho_{\max}\mu)\rceil, so ∂n∗/∂λp≈1/(ρmax​μ)\partial n^{*}/\partial\lambda_{p}\approx 1/(\rho_{\max}\mu). The FOC then requires μs=μl\mu_{s}=\mu_{l}, i.e., both pools have the same service rate. This is generally not achievable for a given BshortB_{\text{short}} because short and long pools serve different request length distributions; in practice Bshort∗B_{\text{short}}^{*} is found numerically by the sweep in Algorithm 1. □\square
